The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2018-12-05.136.1) to *put the question*. These types of motions are known as gagging motions because they end debate and force the House to vote on the question under discussion, which in this case was on [whether to suspend the usual procedural rules](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/divisions/representatives/2018-12-05/6).

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debate/?id=2018-12-05.134.1) introduced by Sturt MP [Christopher Pyne](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/representatives/sturt/christopher_pyne) (Liberal), which means it passed. [Standing orders](https://www.peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/how-parliament-works/parliament-at-work/standing-orders/) are the procedural rules of parliament. ### Motion text > *That so much of the standing orders be suspended as would prevent the resumption of debate on the motion that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018 be read a second time being made an order of the day for a later hour.*
Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018 - Second Reading - Put the question

Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018 - Second Reading - Speed thing along

The majority voted against a motion to amend the usual [second reading motion](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html), which is that the majority should agree with the main idea of the [bill](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r6256) (or, in parliamentary jargon, that the majority should agree to read the bill for a second time). Since this motion was unsuccessful, the original motion will remain unchanged and [can be voted on as is](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/divisions/representatives/2018-12-06/3). ### Motion text > *That all words after “That” be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > *“the House declines to give the bill a second reading, and notes:* > *(1) this unprecedented intervention into markets which will result in higher prices for families and businesses;* > *(2) the Government has abandoned all pretence at being the party of free enterprise and open markets; and* > *(3) the Government has abandoned all proper process, scrutiny and consultation.”* ### What is the main idea of the bill? This bill is part of the Government's package of measures in relation to the electricity sector. For example, the bill sets out three kinds of prohibited conduct in relation to retail prices, the electricity financial contract market and the wholesale electricity market. The remedies included in the bill are graduated, from the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) issuing a public warning notice to the ACCC applying to a court for a pecuniary penalty. The bill also gives new compulsory information gathering powers on the Australian Energy Regulator (AER) and lets the AER share information with other agencies. The Labor Party was concerned with the [speed this legislation](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/debates/?id=2018-12-05.125.2) was being pushed through Parliament by the Coalition Government.

The speaker moved to suspend standing orders to resume debate on the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018, arguing that passing it within 48 hours would allow Senate passage by February 2019 and force energy companies to lower electricity prices, while delay would push passage to at least April 2019.

The speaker argued that Labor opposes the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018 to protect big energy company profits, citing an ACCC finding that three players control 80% of dispatchable generation. They claimed Labor's 45% emission reduction target requires higher electricity prices and will wreck the economy, also tightening rules on farmers' land.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018, which creates prohibitions on retail pricing, contract liquidity, and wholesale bid misconduct to lower electricity costs. The bill establishes a graduated enforcement process—including warning notices, civil penalties up to $10 million or 10% of turnover, and divestment as a last resort—citing ACCC evidence of market dysfunction and price discrepancies such as $411–$832 annual differences for households.

The speaker argued that the government rushed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018 through parliament without proper scrutiny, calling the process chaotic and unacceptable. They criticised the government’s energy policy as a "dog's breakfast" and "harebrained," noting it was the tenth iteration, lacked expert support, and included an unprecedented and possibly unconstitutional divestiture power not recommended by ACCC chairman Rod Sims.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018, arguing that divestiture powers for the ACCC should extend to all markets, not just energy, to address abuses such as supermarkets squeezing agricultural suppliers. The speaker credited former senator Nick Xenophon for championing this power and noted that the court, not a minister, should have the final say on divestiture as a remedy of last resort.

The speaker argued the Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018 would penalise energy companies for misconduct with graduated penalties including divestiture, and criticised the Queensland Labor government for maintaining an effective monopoly, overinvesting $7.3 billion in poles and wires, imposing a six per cent guaranteed return, and failing to pass on a 40 per cent wholesale price reduction to consumers.

The Treasury Laws Amendment (Prohibiting Energy Market Misconduct) Bill 2018 was condemned as the worst, shallowest, and most ill-conceived legislation seen in the parliament, being rushed, unsupported by any inquiry or the ACCC, and opposed by business groups—argued to fail in reducing electricity prices, increase carbon emissions, deter investment, and destroy jobs.

The bill would merge the Federal Circuit Court and the Family Court into a single administrative structure called the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia.
The new court would have two divisions, with one Chief Justice holding a dual commission to both divisions, and would create a consistent case management approach for family law matters.
The bill would not allow decided family law matters to be reopened based on these reforms alone.
Creates the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia as an overarching administrative structure.
Establishes two divisions, with Division 1 continuing the Family Court and Division 2 continuing the Federal Circuit Court.
Provides for a single Chief Justice with a dual commission to both divisions.
Confers family law jurisdiction on both divisions under the Family Law Act 1975.
Allows matters to be transferred between divisions with the approval of the receiving division's Chief Justice or Chief Judge.
Requires the Chief Justice and Chief Judge to work cooperatively on common case management approaches.
Australian families and children involved in family law disputes in the federal court system.

The majority voted against an [amendment](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2018-08-23.20.1) moved by South Australian Senator [Anne Ruston](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/sa/anne_ruston) (Liberal), which means it failed. It would have amended an [original amendment ](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2018-08-23.18.1). ### Amendment > *Omit "15 April 2019", substitute "1 November 2018".* ### Original amendment > *At the end of the motion, add:* > > *"and, in respect of the provisions of the Federal Circuit and Family court of Australia Bill 2018 and the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Consequential Amendments and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2018, the Legal and Constitutional Affairs Legislation Committee report by 15 April 2019".*
Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2018 - Third Reading - Pass the bill

The bill merges the Family Court of Australia and the Federal Circuit Court of Australia into a single Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia, creating a unified administrative structure and a new family law appeal division in the Federal Court, aiming to resolve disputes more quickly and efficiently while addressing a backlog of 21,000 pending cases and rising median trial times.

The Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia (Consequential Amendments and Transitional Provisions) Bill 2018 establishes a new Family Law Appeal Division in the Federal Court from 1 January 2019, transferring most Family Court appellate functions to that division and providing $4 million for harmonising court rules.

Labor opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2018 and related bill, citing no stakeholder consultation, insufficient evidence for clearing 8,000 extra cases, and concerns that the merger would effectively abolish the specialist Family Court by attrition, with appeals heard by a single Federal Court judge lacking family law experience.

The speaker argued that merging the Family Court and Federal Circuit Court would reduce inefficiencies, delays, and costs for families, citing the case of John Edwards, who murdered his two children and himself after custody hearings.

The speaker argued that the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2018 was rushed, lacked adequate consultation, and would effectively abolish the Family Court by not replacing retiring judges. They criticised the Morrison government for underfunding the family law system and failing to consult stakeholders, noting the bill spans 500 pages and amends 125 other bills.

The speaker opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2018, arguing it would gradually abolish the specialist Family Court by merging it with the Federal Circuit Court, halting new appointments to Division 1, and transferring appellate jurisdiction to the Federal Court. They criticised inadequate consultation with stakeholders, reliance on a PricewaterhouseCoopers report, and the government's failure to properly resource the Family Court, which they said caused the backlogs the bill purportedly addresses.

The speaker opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2018, arguing it would abolish the Family Court without proper consultation, and criticised the coalition government for undermining institutions and lacking a governing plan, referencing former Prime Ministers Tony Abbott and Malcolm Turnbull.

The speaker opposed the bills merging the Family Court of Australia into the Federal Circuit Court, arguing the government rushed the process without consulting stakeholders or awaiting the Australian Law Reform Commission’s report, and that the true cause of delays is inadequate resourcing—not court structure—pointing to the Family Court of Western Australia having only five judges, unchanged since 1975 despite population growth.

The speaker opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2018, arguing it would abolish the family law system by stealth rather than fix under-resourcing, and called for adequate funding of courts and legal aid instead of amalgamation.

Labor will oppose the proposed merger of the Family Court and Federal Circuit Court, arguing it would eliminate specialist family-law expertise and endanger domestic-violence victims while providing zero additional funding—despite backlogs growing from 17,000 to 21,000 cases and median trial times rising to 15.2 and 17 months.

The speaker opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2018, arguing it would merge specialist and generalist judges, ignore 33 recommendations from a 2017 inquiry into family law and violence, and prioritise cost-cutting over protecting children and families. They called for proper investment, funding, and replacement of retiring judges instead.

The speaker argued that the government's plan to merge the Family Court and Federal Circuit Court, through the two bills, was based on a rushed six-week desktop review by PwC and a three-week consultation period for a 500-page bill, with virtually no input from experts or the sector, and would eliminate specialist family law expertise, prioritising speed and cost over the best outcomes for children and families. They noted that the Law Council and other bodies opposed the changes, only two government members spoke on the bills, and a Law Reform Commission review was due in March 2019.

Centre Alliance supported the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2018 in the House but not as an endorsement, pending Senate committee review. The speaker raised concerns that removing the Family Court’s appellate function could erode specialist knowledge and that the government’s efficiency focus may overlook quality, noting the claimed 8,305 additional matters resolved per year remains untested.

The speaker supported the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2018 to merge the two family courts, citing current wait times exceeding 15 months and cases taking up to five years, and claimed the merger would finalise an additional 3,000 cases per year and eliminate 35,000 cases being referred to the wrong court.

The speaker opposed the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2018, arguing it would abolish the Family Court against the advice of legal stakeholders and a pending review, and claimed the government ignored the need for more judges and funding. They contrasted the federal approach with the Victorian Labor government’s $152 million investment in a new Bendigo law court.

The speaker argued that the Federal Circuit and Family Court of Australia Bill 2018 merges the Family Court and Federal Circuit Court into a single structure without abolishing the Family Court, creates a new family law appeal division in the Federal Court, and delays the commencement date due to a Senate inquiry. The government allocated $4 million for implementation and predicted $3 million in savings to be reinvested, aiming to reduce waiting times and improve case management.
Social Services Legislation Amendment (Housing Affordability) Bill 2018

The speech argued for the Social Services Legislation Amendment (Housing Affordability) Bill 2017, which introduces an Automatic Rent Deduction Scheme for social housing tenants to prevent rental arrears and homelessness, and amends the National Rental Affordability Scheme to increase flexibility. The social housing system loses over $30 million annually in unpaid rent, and the bill received 32 submissions.

The speaker argued that the Modern Slavery Bill 2018 will require entities with revenue above $100 million to report on supply chain risks, with a central repository and government inclusion as a world-first measure, and noted that no penalties are included initially but a three-year review is planned.
Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-examination of Parties) Bill 2018

The Family Law Amendment (Family Violence and Cross-examination of Parties) Bill 2018 prohibits personal cross-examination of victims by alleged perpetrators in family law proceedings where family violence is alleged, with automatic bans under specified conditions and court discretion otherwise, and requires legal representation and other protective measures.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Personal Income Tax Plan) Bill 2018

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Personal Income Tax Plan) Bill 2018, arguing it delivers tax cuts for low- and middle-income earners, with a maximum benefit of $530 for those earning between $48,000 and $90,000, and a projected surplus in 2019-20. The speech also highlighted a $225 million investment in the Frankston to Baxter train line duplication and criticised Labor's tax policies.
Family Assistance and Child Support Legislation Amendment (Protecting Children) Bill 2018

The member for Dunkley supported the Family Assistance and Child Support Legislation Amendment (Protecting Children) Bill 2017, arguing it would improve child support processes and care arrangements, including terminating agreements when a parent's care falls below 35%, and change immunisation penalties for family tax benefit from an end-of-year supplement reduction to fortnightly withholdings.
Medicare Levy Amendment (National Disability Insurance Scheme Funding) Bill 2017

Supported the Medicare Levy Amendment (National Disability Insurance Scheme Funding) Bill 2017, which raises the Medicare levy by half a percentage point, noting Commonwealth NDIS expenditure will reach $5.3 billion in 2017-18 and $10.8 billion by 2019-20, said the coalition inherited a $55.6 billion funding shortfall from Labor, and said the scheme will transform the lives of around 460,000 Australians with disability, including 105,000 in Victoria.
Competition and Consumer Amendment (Abolition of Limited Merits Review) Bill 2017

The speaker argued that the Competition and Consumer Amendment (Abolition of Limited Merits Review) Bill 2017 should be passed to remove electricity and gas networks' ability to appeal Australian Energy Regulator decisions, noting that 32 of 51 regulator decisions have been challenged since 2008, adding $6.5 billion in consumer costs. The bill also provides $67.4 million in additional funding for the Australian Energy Regulator and was recommended by the Finkel review.
Criminal Code Amendment (Protecting Minors Online) Bill 2017

The Criminal Code Amendment (Protecting Minors Online) Bill 2017 introduces an offence to criminalise acts to prepare or plan to cause harm to, procure, or engage in sexual activity with a person under 16 via a carriage service, citing the case of 15-year-old Carly Ryan and thanking Senator Xenophon for his work.
